references.text: Jesus is asked if he is the Messiah. The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 26:63-64|Matthew 26:63-64] recounts the same scene where the high priest asks Jesus directly if he is the Christ, the Son of God.
The parallel passage in [ref:Mark 14:61-62|Mark 14:61-62] describes the same interrogation where Jesus is asked if he is the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One.

Jesus points out that they will not believe even if he tells them the truth. In [ref:Joh 3:12|John 3:12], Jesus says similar words: "When I have spoken to you about earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I speak to you about heavenly things?"

In [ref:Joh 10:24-25|John 10:24-25], the Jews demand that Jesus state clearly whether he is the Messiah. Jesus answers that he has already told them, but they do not believe – a closely parallel theme to Luke 22:67.

In [ref:Joh 8:45-46|John 8:45-46], Jesus says that because he speaks the truth, they do not believe him. This reflects Jesus' words in Luke 22:67 about how they will not believe even if he tells them.

In [ref:Jer 38:15|Jeremiah 38:15], Jeremiah says to King Zedekiah: "If I tell you this, will you not kill me? And if I give you advice, will you not listen to me?" The same pattern where truth is rejected by those in power.

In [ref:Jes 53:1|Isaiah 53:1], the question is asked: "Who has believed our message?" This prophetic question about unbelief connects to Jesus' observation that they would not believe him no matter what he said.
In [ref:Joh 18:19-24|John 18:19-24], the Gospel of John's version of the interrogation before the high priest is recounted, where Jesus is also questioned about his teaching and identity.
